topic: Software Engineering Principles & The Software Crisis
summary: This foundational topic explores the disciplined genesis of software engineering, contrasting disciplined engineering lifecycles with ad-hoc programming. It analyzes the historical 'Software Crisis' (first identified at the 1968 NATO conference) characterized by budget overruns, delivery delays, unmaintainability, and catastrophic project failures, which drove the evolution of structured engineering standards. Essential product dichotomies (generic off-the-shelf vs customized/bespoke software) are delineated alongside foundational architectural design principles: Abstraction, Modularity, Encapsulation and Information Hiding, Separation of Concerns, High Cohesion versus Low Coupling, the DRY rule, the SOLID design principles (Single Responsibility, Open-Closed, Dependency Inversion), the Principle of Least Privilege, and Defensive Programming.

key_terms.definition: A systematic, disciplined, and measurable approach to the development, operation, maintenance, and evolution of software systems.
The historical phenomenon where software projects routinely ran over budget, missed deadlines, exhibited low reliability, and proved difficult to maintain.
A complete package comprising computer programs, procedures, configuration rules, and all associated technical documentation.
A stand-alone software system developed by a company and sold on the open market, where the developer controls the specification.
Software commissioned by a specific client organization, where the customer owns and dictates the requirement specification.
The technique of representing essential characteristics while hiding non-essential operational and implementation details.
The internal design quality where all responsibilities within a single module are tightly related and directed toward a single well-defined task.
The degree of decoupling between distinct software modules, ensuring changes inside one module do not ripple into others.
The object-oriented design rule stating that a class or module should have only one reason to change.
A coding practice that anticipates incorrect inputs, system failures, and unauthorized requests through proactive validation.

questions.topic: Software Engineering Principles & The Software Crisis
questions.question: In Nile University Final Exam Question 1: What does the term 'software crisis' refer to?
options: All of the above (frequent crashes of software systems, difficulties in meeting schedules and budgets, and lack of qualified software engineers)
Frequent crashes of software systems only
Difficulties in meeting schedules and budgets in software projects only
Lack of qualified software engineers only
questions.explanation: As stated in Nile Exam Question 1: The 'software crisis' (formally identified at the 1968 NATO conference) manifested across multiple interrelated dimensions: catastrophic schedule delays and cost blowouts, poor reliability leading to frequent system crashes, and an acute shortage of trained engineers capable of building large-scale systems.

why_wrong.1: Incomplete; ignores the profound economic schedule and cost failures.
why_wrong.2: Incomplete; ignores the technical quality and personnel crises.
why_wrong.3: Incomplete; only describes the labor symptom without the technical impact.

questions.source: Nile University Final Exam Paper (Type B), Question 1

questions.topic: Software Engineering Principles & The Software Crisis
questions.question: In Nile University Final Exam Question 2: What was a significant reason for the birth of software engineering as a discipline?
options: Failure of large software projects to meet schedule and budget constraints
Demand for faster computers
Increase in the number of software engineers
Evolution of programming languages
questions.explanation: As software projects grew in scale in the 1960s, informal, craft-based programming approaches collapsed. The birth of software engineering as an engineering discipline was precipitated by the systemic failure of large software projects to meet schedule and budget constraints, necessitating rigorous, measurable processes.

why_wrong.1: Hardware speed increased independently via semiconductor advancements (Moore's law).
why_wrong.2: An increase in personnel did not solve the crisis; poor processes made large teams even less efficient (Brooks' Law).
why_wrong.3: New languages were a tool, not the primary historical driver for establishing the discipline.

marking_points: Identifies failure of large projects to meet budget and schedule constraints
questions.source: Nile University Final Exam Paper (Type B), Question 2

questions.topic: Software Engineering Principles & The Software Crisis
questions.question: According to the course notes, how does Software Engineering fundamentally differ from computer programming?
options: Software engineering encompasses the entire software life cycle (requirements, architecture, testing, maintenance, and project management), whereas programming focuses primarily on writing code syntax and algorithms.
Programming is done in teams, while software engineering is strictly an individual effort.
Software engineering only applies to embedded systems, while programming applies to web applications.
There is no distinction; they are completely interchangeable terms.
questions.explanation: Programming is a sub-activity within software engineering. Software engineering is a disciplined, measurable approach spanning feasibility, requirements engineering, architectural design, verification and validation, deployment, maintenance, cost estimation, and multidisciplinary team management.

why_wrong.1: The opposite is true: large-scale software engineering inherently requires coordinated multidisciplinary teams.

marking_points: Covers full life cycle vs code implementation
questions.source: Software Engineering Concepts Lecture Notes, Section 1.3

questions.topic: Software Engineering Principles & The Software Crisis
questions.question: What is the critical difference between a GENERIC software product and a CUSTOMIZED (bespoke) software product regarding specification ownership?
options: In generic products, the specification is owned and controlled by the software developer; in customized products, the specification is owned and controlled by the customer.
In generic products, only open-source code can be used; customized products require assembly language.
Generic products have no user interface, while customized products always have a GUI.
Generic products never require maintenance, while customized products require daily updates.
questions.explanation: Generic products (e.g. Windows, Excel, Photoshop) are sold to the open market, so the vendor determines features and release schedules. Customized products (e.g. Nile University Student Portal, hospital patient records) are commissioned by a single client, who dictates the precise requirements and owns the specification.

why_wrong.In generic products, only open-source co: Most generic software (e.g. Microsoft Office) is proprietary commercial software.
Virtually all consumer generic products feature extensive GUIs.
why_wrong.Generic products never require maintenan: Generic products require continuous updates, security patches, and version upgrades.

questions.source: Software Engineering Concepts Lecture Notes, Section 2.1

questions.topic: Software Engineering Principles & The Software Crisis
questions.question: In software design, what is the desired relationship between COHESION and COUPLING for building robust, maintainable systems?
options: High Cohesion within modules and Low Coupling between modules.
Low Cohesion within modules and High Coupling between modules.
High Cohesion within modules and High Coupling between modules.
Low Cohesion within modules and Low Coupling between modules.
questions.explanation: High cohesion means that elements within a single module collaborate closely on a single, well-defined responsibility (making it easy to understand and maintain). Low coupling means modules depend as little as possible on one another's internal details (preventing bugs from rippling across the system).

why_wrong.1: This is the worst possible architectural anti-pattern ('spaghetti code').
why_wrong.2: High coupling creates rigid, fragile systems that cannot be modified independently.
why_wrong.3: Low cohesion produces bloated, unfocused 'god classes'.

questions.source: Software Engineering Concepts Lecture Notes, Sections 3.5 & 3.6

questions.topic: Software Engineering Principles & The Software Crisis
questions.question: A developer writes a class named 'StudentAccountManager' that handles calculating student fees, generating PDF receipts, and sending payment confirmation emails. Which core software engineering principle is directly violated?
options: Single Responsibility Principle (SRP)
Principle of Least Privilege
Defensive Programming
Abstraction
questions.explanation: The Single Responsibility Principle (SRP) dictates that a class or module should have only one reason to change. The 'StudentAccountManager' has three distinct reasons to change: accounting fee rules, PDF formatting changes, and email notification provider updates. These three concerns should be split into separate cohesive classes.

why_wrong.1: This principle relates to user security access rights, not class responsibilities.
why_wrong.2: This involves input validation and error handling, not module boundaries.
why_wrong.3: Abstraction hides implementation details; the violation here is combining multiple responsibilities.

marking_points: Identifies violation of Single Responsibility Principle
Explains class has multiple reasons to change
questions.source: Software Engineering Concepts Lecture Notes, Section 3.10

questions.topic: Software Engineering Principles & The Software Crisis
questions.question: A university registration module directly instantiates a concrete MySQL database driver class inside its enrollment function rather than interacting through a general 'DatabaseRepository' interface. Which principle does this violate?
options: Dependency Inversion Principle (DIP)
Open-Closed Principle (OCP)
Don't Repeat Yourself (DRY)
Information Hiding
questions.explanation: DIP states: High-level modules should not depend on low-level modules; both should depend on abstractions. Directly coupling the business logic (registration) to a concrete low-level driver (MySQL) prevents switching to PostgreSQL, SQLite, or a mock testing database without rewriting core business logic.

why_wrong.1: OCP deals with extending functionality without modifying existing code.
why_wrong.2: DRY addresses code and knowledge duplication.
why_wrong.3: The driver might still hide internal variables, but the dependency direction is inverted.

marking_points: Identifies violation of Dependency Inversion Principle
Explains high-level business logic must depend on abstractions
questions.source: Software Engineering Concepts Lecture Notes, Section 3.12

questions.topic: Software Engineering Principles & The Software Crisis
questions.question: What does the PRINCIPLE OF LEAST PRIVILEGE dictate in secure software engineering?
options: Every user, process, or system component must operate using only the minimal set of permissions necessary to perform its legitimate task.
Developers should be paid as little as possible to control software costs.
Software should be written without any security controls to maximize speed.
All users must be given root administrator privileges to prevent permission errors.
questions.explanation: The Principle of Least Privilege limits the potential blast radius of an exploit or bug. For instance, in a university portal, a student account should never have database write access to modify grades, and a web worker process should not run with root/administrator OS privileges.

why_wrong.Developers should be paid as little as p: A humorous distractor; least privilege is an architectural security rule, not compensation.
why_wrong.Software should be written without secur: Direct violation of basic security engineering.

marking_points: Explains containment of potential security breaches
questions.source: Software Engineering Concepts Lecture Notes, Section 3.13

questions.topic: Software Engineering Principles & The Software Crisis
questions.question: According to Lehman's Laws of Software Evolution, what happens to a large E-type software system if no proactive refactoring and maintenance effort is applied over time?
options: Continuing Change forces modifications -> Increasing Complexity degrades internal structure -> Quality declines unless actively maintained -> Growth rate slows as maintenance consumed by technical debt
Software automatically refactors itself -> Complexity decreases -> Performance improves exponentially
Software stabilizes permanently and never requires changes after release
Hardware upgrades automatically resolve all software architectural deficiencies
questions.answer: Continuing Change forces modifications -> Increasing Complexity degrades internal structure -> Quality declines unless actively maintained -> Growth rate slows as maintenance consumed by technical debt
questions.explanation: Lehman's First and Second Laws state that an evolving system must continually adapt to its environment or become progressively less satisfactory (Continuing Change), and as it evolves, its complexity increases unless work is done to maintain or reduce it (Increasing Complexity).

Software systems do not self-heal without disciplined human refactoring.
Real-world operational environments change constantly (OS updates, tax laws, business rules).
Hardware upgrades cannot repair architectural tangles or structural rot.

marking_points: Notes Quality decline without proactive refactoring

questions.topic: Software Engineering Principles & The Software Crisis
questions.question: Explain three concrete defensive programming techniques that a software engineer must apply when handling external user input in a web application.
questions.answer:
1. Input Validation & Sanitization: Never trust external input. Validate data types, ranges, lengths, and formats against strict whitelists before processing (e.g. rejecting SQL injection or script tags).
2. Graceful Error Handling & Exceptions: Anticipate null values, lost database connections, and unexpected states using try-catch blocks and structured error logging, rather than letting the application crash or leak stack traces to users.
3. Fail-Safe Defaults: In security checks and state decisions, default to a safe, unprivileged state (e.g., deny access by default if permission checks fail or timeout).
questions.explanation: Defensive programming ensures system robustness, availability, and security by assuming that inputs will occasionally be malformed, malicious, or unavailable.
marking_points: Mentions structured exception handling without crashing
Mentions fail-safe defaults or rejecting unauthenticated states
questions.source: Software Engineering Concepts Lecture Notes, Section 3.14

case_studies.scenario: A fast-growing fintech startup in Abuja built an automated loan disbursement application using ad-hoc programming techniques. A single monolithic script named 'LoanHandler.py' (over 4,000 lines of code) parses JSON web requests, calculates borrower credit risk, runs SQL queries against a PostgreSQL database, generates PDF loan contracts, and calls external SMS and payment APIs. Over 6 months, every minor interest-rate formula change inadvertently corrupted customer SMS notifications and created intermittent database connection pool exhaustions, causing the system to crash during peak morning hours.

sub_questions.topic: Software Engineering Principles & The Software Crisis
sub_questions.question: From a software engineering perspective, how should the architecture of 'LoanHandler.py' be diagnosed regarding cohesion and coupling?
options: It exhibits critically Low Cohesion (combining unrelated responsibilities) and High Coupling (tight internal dependencies between calculations, database, and third-party APIs).
It exhibits High Cohesion and Low Coupling, indicating an ideal architecture.
It exhibits High Cohesion because all code is located conveniently in one file.
It demonstrates proper Separation of Concerns because all banking tasks are together.
sub_questions.explanation: Cohesion measures internal focus: a single class doing UI, risk math, database queries, PDF generation, and SMS calls has very low cohesion. Coupling measures interdependency: changes in risk math rippling into SMS crashes proves tight coupling. Placing everything in one file is an anti-pattern, not cohesion.

why_wrong.2: Common student blunder: confusing file compactness with functional cohesion.

sub_questions.topic: Software Engineering Principles & The Software Crisis
sub_questions.question: Propose an architectural refactoring plan for this loan system using the Single Responsibility Principle (SRP) and Dependency Inversion Principle (DIP). Identify the specific modules that should be created.
sub_questions.answer:
1. Apply Single Responsibility Principle (SRP) by decomposing the monolithic script into four distinct cohesive services:
   a. CreditRiskEvaluator: purely handles interest calculation and borrower risk rules.
   b. LoanRepository: handles database persistence, transactions, and connection pools.
   c. ContractGenerator: handles PDF rendering from loan parameters.
   d. NotificationService: manages SMS and email dispatch.
2. Apply Dependency Inversion Principle (DIP):
   - High-level loan orchestrator depends on abstract interfaces (e.g. IPaymentGateway, INotificationProvider, ILoanRepository) rather than concrete third-party SDKs.
   - This allows mocking the SMS API and database during unit tests and enables swapping payment providers without altering business calculations.
sub_questions.explanation: Applying SRP and DIP isolates failure domains, so interest rule changes cannot break notifications.
marking_points: Decomposes into distinct modules (Risk, Database/Repo, Contract, Notification)
Applies SRP by giving each module one reason to change
Applies DIP by introducing abstract interfaces for third-party services and repositories

case_studies.scenario: Nile University's IT directorate is tasked with deploying an automated biometric examination attendance verification platform across 4 campus faculties. The university is debating whether to purchase a generic, commercial off-the-shelf attendance product from an international vendor or commission a customized (bespoke) system developed specifically for Nile University's academic regulations and biometric hardware.

sub_questions.topic: Software Engineering Principles & The Software Crisis
sub_questions.question: What is the primary risk Nile University faces if it chooses the GENERIC commercial off-the-shelf attendance product rather than a bespoke solution?
options: The university does not control the software specification, forcing the university to either compromise on its unique institutional examination rules or incur high customization and integration costs.
Generic software cannot run on modern x86 or ARM computer hardware.
Generic software is legally prohibited from storing student matriculation numbers.
Generic software developers always retain the right to delete university grades.
sub_questions.explanation: In generic software, the vendor owns and controls the specification to satisfy general market demand. When an institution has unique local workflows (e.g. Nile University's specific continuous assessment weighting or biometric clearance gates), generic software often requires awkward workarounds or costly custom integration layers.

why_wrong.Generic software cannot run on modern ha: Commercial software is typically designed for standard modern hardware architectures.
Data protection compliance depends on data processing agreements, not whether software is generic.

marking_points: Highlights mismatch with unique institutional rules
sub_questions.source: Software Engineering Concepts Lecture Notes, Section 2.1

sub_questions.topic: Software Engineering Principles & The Software Crisis
sub_questions.question: In the bespoke architecture, examination invigilators are given tablet devices to scan student fingerprints at exam hall entrances. Applying the Principle of Least Privilege, what database access permissions should the invigilator tablet application possess?
options: Read-only access to verify student enrollment and biometric templates, and append-only permission to record attendance timestamp records for that specific exam session.
Full read-write administrator access to all tables including student GPAs, fee payments, and exam question databases.
Direct DROP and ALTER TABLE SQL privileges to reset the database between exams.
Zero database access of any kind; all validation must be done purely via paper printouts.
sub_questions.explanation: Under the Principle of Least Privilege, the tablet app needs only to check who is eligible (read enrollment) and mark who showed up (append timestamp log). Granting write or admin access to academic records creates severe security risks (e.g. grade tampering if a tablet is stolen).

Massive security vulnerability violating least privilege.
Catastrophic DDL permissions that could destroy university data.
Defeats the entire purpose of deploying an automated biometric tablet platform.

marking_points: Grants minimal necessary read and append permissions
Denies modification access to unrelated academic records
sub_questions.source: Software Engineering Security & Least Privilege Principles
